That, in the opinion of this House, it is desirable that in the best interests of the Dairy Industry and of the public generally, the manufacture and importation of oleomargarine should be discontinued in Canada after September first next.
The Government would like to have the views of hon. members of the House on that subject, and I would be agreeable to promising consideration of this resolution on Monday next, if members of the House wish to have it taken up at that time. In regard to the other motion, I think I will have to ask my hon friends to allow the Government opportunity to consider what would be the best time to consider it.

speechtext: I have read the resolution which was submitted by the Government, and it distinctly states that next Monday will be available for private members' resolutions. maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. COPP CORRECTION OF REPORT CONCERNING REPARATION CLAIMS
speechtext:
I desire to take this opportunity, as a matter of privilege, of correcting a statement attributed to me in a report appearing in the Montreal Gazette, and possibly in other newspapers throughout the country:
Mr. Copp stated that reparation claims amounting to $22,000,000 had been filed. Some of these claims had already been satisfied.
I desire to state most explicitly that I made no such statement as that, and if hon. members will refer to unrevised Hansard, page 1735, they will see exactly what I did say. I do not, for a moment, suggest that the reporter wilfully made this statement; but I do not want the statement spread broadcast throughout the country, because there have been filed in the department a large number of these claims, none of which has been paid. Those who have filed reparation claims, if some had been paid, would naturally be surprised that all the claims had not been considered at one and the same time. I want to make it clear that no claims have been considered or paid by the department.

What does the Civil Aviation consist of?
Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM (Minister of Militia and Defence) : The Civil Aviation consists almost altogether of work done for the other departments, such as fire ranging, work done for other provinces, and survey work.
How much for other provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The province of Quebec last year erected buildings worth, if I remember aright, $20,000 at Roberval, and the department went fifty-fifty They took the buildings as the province's share, and they did the fire ranging for the province. Ontario paid $50,000 for her share, and British Columbia $20,000.
If this was worked up by the provinces, why do the Dominion authorities contribute anything to it? The provinces in some cases, are much better off than the Dominion authorities.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
It is one of these
peculiar situations where the federal Government participates, as it does sometimes in the matter of education. It is an experiment in collaboration with the provinces. The imperial authorities presented by the federal Government $5,000,000 worth of aviation equipment, and the work could not very well be undertaken by all the provinces unless they purchased their own equipment, so we gave it to them. The federal government undertook for a time to do this work. This year we have informed the provinces as well as the other departments of the Dominion government that if they want work done we shall be glad to undertake it, provided they pay the cost of doing it.
Is this reduction in connection with civil aviation, or with what might be described as the military branch?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Both. There is a misconception as to what the department really

intends to do with the Air Force. It was divided into civil and military. As a matter of fact, if Canada were in a position to enter largely into a field of this kind I should be rather inclined to leave the service as it was, under an air board attached to the department. But the force is comparatively small, and, in my opinion, must for a few years at least be in a merely experimental state. Consequently it and the Militia Department are being brought under the Department of National Defence. The Militia Department Is not absorbing any of these entities; the idea is simply to amalgamate the three services so as, if possible, to reduce executive expenses. There has been a considerable difference of opinion, and not without reason, as to whether it was better to keep the Air Force outside the military branch than to bring it into the Department of National Defence. If we had a large organization and anticipated a large expenditure and a great development in the Air Force, it might be as well to leave it by itself. But I take it for granted that we are not in a position to develop any considerable organization just now in Canada. Furthermore, when civil aviation has reached a certain point in its development, private companies will largely undertake this work. I may not be in accord with hon. members, but I do believe that the Dominion is not prepared to enter upon any large scheme of government-owned and operated civil aviation service. I think that we should rather, for a time, act as instructors, allowing private companies and the provinces to get into the business themselves and look after their own affairs. That part of the work will be carried on under the new arrangement precisely as was done previously, and we hope this year to carry on all the civil aviation work we did last year. We are asking, however, that the provinces and the other departments of the Government pay the costs of operation, and we can assure them that the work will be done just as thoroughly as heretofore.

There are two changes, I understand. The minister purposes to ask for larger contributions from the provinces for the services they get, and' he also intends to assess the other departments for the benefits they derive from the organization. That accounts, I presume, for the substantial diminution in the estimates?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
It will account for some of it; the amounts are not overly large.

Supply-Air Board

I hope the minister will not feel discouraged when I say that I concur in the attitude that he has taken towards this estimate, and I sincerely hope that my fidelity to the estimate will not alter his, and that we shall not find him coming back with another one later on. Very manifestly it would not be the part of economy, and consequently not the part of wisdom-because it would not carry with it efficiency-if all the provinces should commence individually air force organizations, at least while the science is in the experimental stage. You could scarcely conceive a greater waste of effort and money than would eventuate from such a course as that. The Dominion is the possessor of the equipment for this work. The work is almost wholly experimental, and undoubtedly can be done better by the Dominion Government in co-operation with the provinces than it ever could be done by the provinces themselves, each acting on its own initiative and separately. For myself, I have the utmost confidence-well, I will not say that, but at any rate I have some confidence-that very considerable results will be achieved, and that ere long, in the matter of forest fire protection. I may be wrong, but I think that in discussion of the estimates of the Interior Department this session the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) explained how a very considerable saving had been effected already on the timber areas in British Columbia by the adoption of this method of preservation. The department is therefore well advised as respects that matter, if there were nothing else to influence them, not to abandon the Air Force work. In regard to survey work for the Interior and other departments, although I am not sure that it has yet reached the point where it might be described as being a success, nevertheless it has not been brought to the point where failure is evident. There is in this connection also an opening for real service and real economy. For these reasons I ,'up-port the attitude of the minister and hope he will not abandon it.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
My right hon. friend
(Mr. Meighen) is right. I imagine it will not be very long before a good deal of the work on the ground in the matter of fire protection is done away with. Most of the work is done in the air; in the Winnipeg district that is the case at the present time. The department received a letter the other day from the engineers, who are preparing their report on the deep waterways, informing us that the air service had been of inestimable value to them in donig their work.

I understand that the High River station has rendered a great service in saving the Dominion forest reserve in that district, or at least in the vicinity, from destruction by fire during the past year. Is it the intention of the department to do away with this station at that point?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We hope to bo able to do the work, to put it mildly, as thoroughly as it was done last year, and if possible to do more work.

I should like a more definite statement from the minister. I have had letters from the boards of trade, not only in my own constituency but in the constituency of my hon. friend from Macleod (Mr. Coote), protesting against any diminution on the part of the federal government of its activities in this matter. They are opposed to such a course for more reasons than just the preservation of the forest as such. The preservation of the forest is absolutely essential to the irrigation projects now under way in southern Alberta, and we protest most earnestly against any diminution on the part of the Dominion government of the good work that has been done in the past. I should be glad if the minister would state definitely whether or not that station is to be maintained.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I cannot for the life of me see how the report got out that the air station at High River was to be abolished. I received a great many communications myself, and delved all around the department, but without avail, to find any one who knew how the suggestion had got out. The station will be maintained, as I said before, and possibly more work will be done than was done last year.
Did the minister say it was the intention to have the provincial governments pay for this work in the different provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
We are asking the provincial governments to pay the cost of operation in connection with any work we do for them. They were informed last August of this decision on the part of the department.
Supply-Air Board
It would not seem right that the provinces which have not got their natural resources should have to pay those expenses in the same proportion as the provinces which have.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Three provinces have
asked us to perform the work-Quebec, Ontario and British Columbia, and I am afraid the question of natural resources does not come up in connection with these provinces.
How much of this work was done in each of the provinces last year, and at what cost?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The cost of the operations at Vancouver was $63,958.
That would be for the province of British Columbia?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No, some of that was for the Dominion. About $20,000 was paid by the British Columbia government. At High river the cost was $120,669. Quite a large proportion of that was for construction of the wireless station there and other work in connection with it.
Would that $120,000 be charged wholly against the province, or would part of it be borne by the Dominion?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: All by the Dominion, I think. At Victoria. Beach, Man., the expenditure was $66,870; at Sioux Lookout, $35,574; the Ontario government reimbursed the federal government $15,000 of that expenditure; Roberval, Quebec, $31,099; Dartmouth, Nova Scotia, $43,322; Ottawa, $59,512; Haileybury, $1,049.

Is the
High river station the only one in Alberta? I think most of the timber is in the northern part of the province.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: This is the only station in Alberta. Last year a machine was sent to Jasper for a short time.
Is it the intention of the department to extend the work into northern Alberta in view of the fact that this method is more efficient than the other?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am afraid we cannot promise much extension of the work with the estimate where it is.

What work was done at
Dartmouth, Nova Scotia?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is a station which was used largely for sea-planes. It was in use during the war. The work performed at that station was not very extensive last year, most of the expenditure representing maintenance.
Does not the minister think that that station should be closed?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We will consult with the provincial government.
I did not catch from the minister his report for the province of Saskatchewan.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
It would be hard to
catch. There was no request from Saskatchewan, and no work was done.

I am pleased to hear the minister state that fire prevention work over our timber areas would be done by aeroplane, and I merely wish to add that that is the thought which was in the mind3 of our people here when we were talking about the militia estimates, that the air service will do the work in future instead of the militia.

I think the plan is
right of assessing against the provinces the services performed for them, as certain provinces will require more service than others and they should pay proportionately. But what is the value of collecting from the various departments for any services rendered in regard to work formerly done by those departments? It will entail all sorts of bookkeeping and an additional cumbersome organization.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
It is a matter of arrangement between the departments. As Minister of Railways my experience was that whenever anything was to be carried some members of the government got it into their heads that my railways ought to carry it for nothing, and my department was made the goat, and at the end of the year the real showing of the railways was not evidenced in the report. So far as the Dominion treasury is concerned it does not make any difference. But for years past the militia estimates have been severely criticised and economy has been urged. What I had in my mind was this. For example, if the Interior Department wanted to appropriate $50,000 for fire rangers, and this Air Force were not in existence, the Department of the Interior would have to pay for the men engaged in the work. If we do the work for the Interior Depart-

Supply-Air Board
ment, then the Department of National Defence should not he charged with an expenditure, that ought to be made by the Department of the Interior. I wanted to show the actual expenditure of my department.

The minister has been
pretty frank. The only object he has in mind is to keep the defence estimates down, and thereby be able to show that the Government has kept its pledge.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: If the other men do the same thing it will be all right.

I know he is all right. The Intercolonial Railway when it was operated by the Department of Railways was made the goat-it was supposed to carry everything free. That was all remedied by the late government, so this government will not have to face that condition again.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not see any evidence of that anywhere. I will bring that up on the Orders of the Day.

That has all been cured. This is a case of the government service. You might just as well take any other department and where it does anything that was formerly done by another department charge it up to that other department. That would apply to the Departments of the Interior, Militia,-to every department of the Government. You would have a sort of interchange bookkeeping system that would be the most cumbersome and unmanageable in the world. If the Department of Militia and Defence is performing certain services, those services are not performed for particular individuals, as was the case with the railway service in former years; those services are performed for the whole nation. I see the object the minister has in view, but that is no good reason for adopting this course as relating to the Air Force. I submit the same plan should be followed as in all other departments of the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I do not want to block
these estimates, Mr. Chairman, but I submit that the man who is put at the head of a department should run it on business principles, and if some other department wants his department to spend $50,000, that other department ought to ask for the appropriation and make the necessary transfer. In a large departmental store every branch is on its own footing, and if it
lends anything to another branch it gets credit and the other branch is debited with it. That is the only way in which the head of such an institution can tell which branch is doing business properly and which is not. Now, if one branch of the government service is to be charged with work done for three or four other branches, it may look like a very extravagant branch when it is perhaps the most economical of the lot. I had my difficulties with the Department of Militia and Defence when I was Minister of Railways with reference to the transport of troops and so forth. I insisted that they should use their own railway and that they should pay for it when they did. Why should the Department of Railways carry troops for the Department of Militia, run up its deficit and keep down the expenditures of the Department of Militia?-I am referring to it, of course, from the point of view of the presentation of the results of the work of each department to the House and to the public.

What the public want to know is what the Air Force is costing. The minister proposes to charge each department for any special work he does for it, and there will be no way of ascertaining what the Air Board costs. That is a way of camouflaging it, of disguising it, by making it appear, if only the total is looked at and no examination is made beneath the surface, that the expenditure has been reduced. If I understand the minister's statement aright, the whole operations of the Air Board are to be continued. I have not heard that any are to be cut off, unless it be that work heretofore done for the provinces on the principle of fifty-fifty is now to be done entirely at provincial expense. That would involve a reduction, but only a very slight one, because the amount contributed by the provinces was very small indeed. But the whole work is evidently to go on and the whole expense will probably be there. All the salaries are continued-$75,000 for this year just the same as last year. What I object to in the system is this: certain newspapers in this country when these estimates were published proclaimed that the minister had performed a wonderful service; that he had cut down the Air Board estimates by some $600,000 or $700,000. But it is evident that the whole work is to be continued; there is no real cut in the estimate, no real reduction in the expense. A good many promises of reduction were made, but according to the
Supply-Air Board

statement given this afternoon by the minister the work is to be carried on as formerly, though instead of charging it to the Air Board, where it should be charged, it is to be spread out over various departments, with the result that the public will not know what the Air Force is costing. Now, last year the Air Board performed services for the Department of Marine and Fisheries; coastal patrols to prevent poaching and fishing out of season; transportation of spawn; rapid transportation to inaccessible points in British Columbia. That is all charged against the Air Board; we know what the Air Board is costing. Last year certain work was performed by the Air Board for the Department of Agriculture: securing vertical and oblique photographs of mosquito-infested areas in proximity to Vancouver. That was charged to the Air Board. If that work is continued it will be charged to the Department of Agriculture and we shall not know what the Air Board is costing. Last year the Air Board did work for the Department of the Interior; oblique photography of deltas, lakes, etc., for map purposes; also forest fire protection work, forest reconnaissance, and inspection of burnt areas from the air All that work was charged to the Air Board, so that the people know what the cost is. Now, the minister proposes to charge it to the Department of Interior, and no one will know what the Air Board costs. Last year the Air Board did work for the Department of Customs-here is a new avenue of work for it: patrols to prevent smuggling of drugs from the East into Canada. I think it was brought out in a debate we had in the House a few days ago that a good many of these drugs gain access to Canada by being thrown overboard in casks and barrels and picked up by fishing boats near the coast and brought ashore. That has been very largely stopped through the efforts of the Air Board. The activities of the board in this respect are now to be charged to the Department of Customs. I submit that the proposal is wrong. The air service is now a very important item in the budget of every country. Last year the vote for this purpose in the United States was $95,000,000; I think it is about the same this year, or perhaps larger. In Great Britain the amount spent is tremendous. Australia and New Zealand have made their first expenditure in air service, and I think every civilized nation has done likewise. The work is experi-
mental as yet and the people are curious to know just what it costs. It is an expensive service, there is no doubt about that. Machines are costly; repairs run into large sums; high-class men have to be well paid-flying operations from the beginning to end are vastly expensive. I submit that the estimates last year and the year before were pared down to a very . modest and reasonable amount, one quite in keeping with our general expenditure and our general requirements. This year there is a change in method, but there is going to be no change in result; in fact, any change made under the proposal of the minister will be detrimental. We know to-day just what the Air Board costs, what officials will be retained, and what salaries are to be paid. By the way, I understand that the resignation of the only official who acted in a purely honorary capacity and who gave wonderful service has been accepted since the new Government took office. I refer to Colonel O. M. Biggar, who since the Air Board was constituted had been its deputy chairman and gave his services without remuneration. About a year ago he tendered his resignation to me when I was acting as chairman of the board, but I did not accept it; he was too valuable a man. But I believe that the new administration has accepted his resignation, although he was the only unpaid official in the air service, and his work was extremely important and exceedingly well done, as is everything which Colonel Biggar does. On the whole I cannot take exception to the amount which the Government proposes to expend, but I do think it should be put just as plainly as it was last year; the House and the country should know what we propose to spend. It should all be in the estimates; let us know what the Air Board is costing Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is so easy that I am surprised that my hon. friend should bring it up. If he had kept in mind what I said about the departmental store he would know and the country would know exactly what the air service costs. If there are to be credits from other departments they will appear as well.
Why not put them all in one?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
They will be in one, but if there are any receipts from provinces or from other departments, they will be shown. The estimates will not be changed. Last year there were receipts from provinces.

Supply-Air Board

Then the information the minister gave the committee a few moments ago was very misleading, or I am very dense. I understood, because he put it in very plain language, that all that was done for the various departments was to be paid for by them. Now he leads me to believe that his present estimate is the whole expenditure on the air service. I do not know which is right. If the amount stated in this estimate, $1,000,000, is to be the total expenditure, reduced by $625,000 from last year, the minister should not maintain his whole staff as he is doing. He has cut down 33 per cent of his expenditure. I assume, then, that he will cut down at least one-third of his air operations. One may reasonably suppose that a third of his staff would likewise be cut down. But the first information which he gave to the leader of the Opposition was the correct information, that he proposed to continue the operations. He is now trying to camouflage it by letting each department charge itself with the amount which the service performed for that department represents. What the committee want to know, and what the people of this country want to know, is what the whole cost of the air service is going to be; if $1,000,000 is going to be the expenditure, let us know it, and if every department is going to add to that amount, let us know that also.

I will remind the minister, before he rises, that I pointed out the difference between the $1,000,000 and the $1,625,000, and after he told me there were to be charges against departments and against governments, I said "That accounts for this difference," to which he replied that it accounted in part.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: To a very small extent, I think I said.

To any extent at all, it contradicts what the minister said, because if all the charges are in the $1,000,000 and the credits come in from the departments, they would not account for one dollar of the difference.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Hon. gentlemen seem to object to the way in which I have brought this estimate down, and the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) talks of "camouflage." There is no camouflage about it at all. He talks of not reducing the staff, but I am inclined to think he knows better. He knows because there have been many people to see him about
it. Practically all the temporary staff of the Air Force, or at all events the great majority, have gone now and $35,000 will be saved in temporary employees who were paid out of the Air Board vote. There is $35,000 saved before we begin to reorganize.
First, that is not a correct statement; secondly, it is an unfair statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Absolutely correct and perfectly fair.
No one has seen me on this subject, not a single individual from the minister down to the lowest official, and there has not been one letter-not a word.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: They have been to see me.

What I state is absolutely correct. Here is the estimate, $75,000, for this year just the same as last year. If you have cut down your operations this year one-third, why do you need the same vote as last year? I maintain that you are not cutting it down except on paper. You are really going to continue the same operations. I hope you will, but I say that you are trying to camouflge the expenditure. What about the resignation of Colonel Biggar, may I ask?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I think this matter was explained by myself in the House on a former occasion, but when the militia estimates come up my hon. friend always takes great pains to make it embarrassing for the gentlemen themselves as well as for the minister, when any person retires of his own accord or is retired. The hon. member for South Wellington is no better friend of Colonel Biggar than I am. As I said in this House some weeks ago, Colonel Biggar worked for this
4 p.m. department gratis as vice-president and as soon as I came into the department he told me that he had offered his resignation some time before, and he offered it again. I asked him to retain his position for a while until we discovered what we were going to do. Then, when the time came to discuss the question of amalgamation, Colonel Biggar again offered his resignation, and I accepted it.

Has his place been
filled?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
His place has not been filled.
Supply-Air Board
Does the minister propose to fill his place?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: If we have the reorganization, there will be no place to fill.
Is the Air Board as now constituted to be continued?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I think my hon. friend has probably not read over the bill. The Air Board is not to be continued.

How is it to be
operated-as a branch of the Defence Department? Is it to be a separate branch, and if so, who is to be the presiding genius, and what assistants will he have?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
It is very difficult to
give these details before the reorganization is at least partially completed. The bill for bringing about the reorganization has not yet become law. As I explained some time ago, the Air Board will be an integral part of the Department of Defence: it will not be absorbed by the Department of Militia and Defence. I think I can say to the House that practically all the technical officers and most of the staff will be taken into the new Department of Defence. We shall have a Director of Aviation, and perhaps one or two assistants. The technical officers we have now will be part of the Department of Defence, and not on the outside but on the inside.

I see that
the sum voted for salaries last year was $75,000. The minister says that he is getting rid of temporary employees to the amount of $35,000, but there is no corresponding reduction in this item. Why is that?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That was not under this item. That was not my explanation.
Out of what vote were the temporary help paid last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Out of the general vote
for the Air Force.
What were these people doing who were in temporary service?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am informed they were doing technical and equipment service.

I do not know just
what that means. What is it? Repairing machines?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Aeronautical engineering staff, and stores. In addition, there were a lot of temporary clerks, as there are in every department. They were carried in the main bulk vote to the amount of $35,000.

Why was that service
necessary last year and not this year? The officer of the department will know.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Because the staff does
not need to be so large. In the first place, we are amalgamating, and we expect to get along with fewer quarter-masters and accountants, for instance. We expect to save something there. Then we have not so much money to spend. Some of the details of operation will be cut out, although the main work will be carried on.

I do not just get my
mind around that. The bill is not through yet for the amalgamation. I have always contended the minister did not need the bill, but he says he does. The bill is not yet through, and if these temporary employees are all being let out in anticipation of the bill going through, if they are away from the service now, they are not needed there, of course. There must be something that was done last year that is not being done this year, and I am anxious to find out what service that is. What would the amalgamation have to do with the aeronautical engineering service, for instance? Nothing in the world. The men repairing aeroplanes are not going to be any different whether the department is called National Defence, or Air Board.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
We will be doing less
flying; there will be less of this kind of work.

What flying service is
being cut down or eliminated?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
At the present time
there is little or no training being done at Camp Borden. The camp will be opened up a little later on, but not to the extent it has been, probably.

But what service is
going to be reduced? There would not be any training at Camp Borden last year more than this year. What service is being cut down or taken away?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
My information is that
flying is being cut down proportionately. All I have stated in the House here is in

Supply-Air Board
reference to the main work of civil aviation in the department. We hope to carry on the work that is being done for the provinces this year, but the other work is being cut in every particular, or we could not make this reduction.

That is to say, there
is going to be less aeroplane service for the protection of our own forests?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I did not say that.

The hon. minister said that outside of what we were doing for the provinces all the rest was cut proportionately. Now, we are not protecting our own forests for the provinces, we are protecting them for ourselves. It follows, therefore, that that is being cut, or else the minister was not accurate. The minister's reply from his seat would indicate that he is not cutting that service. Then what is it? Is it the survey service for the Interior Department or for the Customs Department? What is it that is being reduced?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I merely gave my hon. friend one item. We are not building any stations this year. We built quite a number last year.
I presume when stations are built they are built, and it would hardly be economy to tear them down. That accounts for some. Can the minister account for anything else?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My hon. friend is very technical.
Not at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am not in the witness box. I am giving the House all the information I can give. We are doing this thing at Camp Borden, and cutting the expense in every quarter, without interfering with the special service of the organization.
I asked him if he was cutting at one quarter and he indignantly denied it.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The right hon. member must not put words in my mouth. He is not catechising a witness in the witness box, and I am not going to permit him, even if he has been Prime Minister, to put words in my mouth which I have not used. I have answered the question fairly and thoroughly, and if talking and manufacturing in his own mind questions that he did not put, and answers that he did not receive, amuses him, let him go on.
The minister may not be a witness in the witness box; I did not say he was. But he is a minister of the Crown in Canada, subject to inquiry in the House as to his estimates.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Surely.

I asked him was what being reduced; I desire specific answers, and I am entitled to them. I am not demanding any answer because I was Prime Minister or anything on account of myself, other than that I am a member of Parliament, with the rights of a member of Parliament. The minister wants to get away by simply saying "Oh, I am reducing, I am cutting down expense," with the hope that the committee will get the impression that this is a great matter of economy on his part without reduction of service. Then I asked him what service he was reducing, and his reply was that he was reducing all-round proportionately. Then he said that he was not reducing the service to the provinces, but was reducing the rest. I am not putting words in his mouth. These are his own words. I said he must be reducing the service for the protection of our forests. From his seat he disputed that. Where have I put words in his mouth? Not at all. He is not reducing that service. He has so answered. I hope that answer is right and that he is not reducing the service. What service is he reducing? He said "we built some stations last year, and did not need to build them this year." That accounts for some reduction, but it is not a reduction of service.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It is a reduction iq money.

Very good. I have accepted that. That is quite clear. We understand that. If that accounts for the whole reduction, all right, I am satisfied, but if it is something else I want to know specifically what it is, and I would like the minister to explain on what ground I am not entitled to an answer. I would like to know specifically what is being reduced, what has enabled him to do it, and where is the service that is going to be left, and why?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I have answered these questions several times. The right hon. gentleman does not expect to get answers in dollars and cents in every detail. He knows that is impossible. We do be-
Supply-Air Board

lieve that when we get the department properly organized, if we are allowed to do it, we can perform the essential service that we did last year at a much less expense than last year. We are cutting out at the present time training at Camp Borden. We will have the instruction school at Camp Borden later on I hope, and without giving the details in every particular, as no person can know at the present time just what they will be, we are undertaking to carry on the work with the reduction of $625,000, and I hope we will be able to do it; I believe we will. The work to be done by the different departments of the Government will depend on the requisitions of those departments of Government. Just at the moment I cannot tell in what I am going to reduce the work done for the different departments of government. I may reduce some and increase others; that will depend on the requisitions the different departments make. But we do believe we can carry on the service and give satisfaction to the provinces for $1,000,000. When the department is fully reorganized, and we get it in working shape, we will be able to give details, but at present it is impossible to give them, because we have not our organization perfect.

I wish to ask one or two specific questions. Is it the intention of the department to maintain the same forest patrol in the railway belt in British Columbia, and in what is known as the Peace River block? Take the railway belt-

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, in the railway belt.
Is it intended to maintain the same patrol service at Vancouver in connection with the Customs Department and the other miscellaneous services rendered by the board and the department last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The Customs Department have already asked that the patrols be maintained, and we believe we can maintain them.

The minister resists
giving us the details. He says "I am cutting down the amount, and you must leave it to me to make the saving where I can." I submit, the minister is not treating the committee properly. He can give many more details than he has given. Here is an estimate of $1,525,000 Canadian Air

Force and Civil Aviation. His officers cut it down to $907,500. Note the "$500." They have it down to a matter of a hundred dollars. It is not as if it were reduced to a round $1,000,000, but it is reduced to $907,500. The officers of this department have the details making up that $907,500. They have the corresponding details making up the $1,525,000 of last year, and those details will show where the reductions are in each case, and the minister or his officers can tell this committee just how the reductions are made, whether by reduction of service, or how and just how much of that is due to the fact that the stations have been built, and how much is due to something else, and what the other things are.

Furthering what my right hon. friend has just said, the item of $907,500 has not been put there by chance or guess. It represents something. Last year the same item was $1,525,000, and we know what it represented. It was stated in the estimates last year that $700,000 of it was for civil aviation; $825,000 of it was for the Air Board for the military end of the service.
Of the $700,000 the items were as follows:
Flying for other Government Departments	 $365,000
They charged it all up to the Air Board last year.
Experimental Flying Research..	..	$ 50,000
Upkeep of equipment	 80,000
Acquisition and equipment of civil
air stations	 220,000
Total	  $715,000
Less amounts for operation on account of Ontario and Quebec	..	35,000
Total sum required	 $680,000
In addition, there is an item of $20,000 for licensing, inquiry into accidents, survey of air routes, etc. This makes a total of $700,000. When we come to the military side of the Air Board work, we have a total of $825,000, according to the following details:
28-day refresher course for 190 flying
officers	 $380,000
28-day refresher course for 50 ground
officers	 22,000
3 months' course for 400 mechanics..	240,000
Spare parts	 100,000
Seaplane training	 60,000
Provincial executives		23,000
Total	 $825,000
That is what Parliament voted last year.

Supply-Air Board
The hon. member has given us the full details of the expenditure of 1921-22. Would he be good enough to keep right on and give us the details for this year?
That is what I am trying to find out.
Has the hon. member the details?
No, I have not.
The hon. member has those of last year, wherever he got them. Will he tell us where he got those details from?

I had them in the
House last year. I was questioned on them.
Not those details.
If I was asked questions on them, I certainly had them before me, because this is the memorandum that I presented to the House last year when my estimates were before the House.
Does it not belong to the department, and not to the hon. member? What right has the hon. member to that memorandum? It belongs to the department.

I have a right to it, and there is the duplicate of it in the department. I think there is a duplicate of it at this moment in the desk of the minister. If there is not, there should be. I want to know what is going to be done with the money for the current year. There is a lump item of $900,000, and not a single detail of what they are going to do with it. The least the minister could do would be to give to the committee some idea of what the expenditure is going to be. He must know how that item of $900,000 is made up. It will not take more than a minute or two to give it to the committee, and the committee is entitled to the information.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I made the explanation a moment ago. It was all very well for my hon. friend last year to have the estimate of what he was going to do, because he was carrying on the Air Board just as it was before. All he had to do was to sit down and make out the estimates in detail. He knows, and the committee, knows that, on account of our reorganization, which I hoped would have taken place some weeks ago, but which has been delayed, it is impossible to sit down and make
out those details, because we have not got into our new organization, we have not our departments together. The Air Board itself is not in a position to sit down and make out all those details, because it does not know whether it will be operated. Let me point this out to my hon. friend. I could give him some figures in connection with stations, not details, because, under present conditions, it is impossible to make out the details for the coming year under present conditions. We propose to keep the estimates within $1,000,000 and to give the essential services.
Will that include the work which the Air Board is going to do for other departments?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
That will depend whether I can get any money out of the other departments or not. The figures to which I referred are; in round numbers:
Headquarters	 $32,440
Vancouver air station	 81,560
High river air station	 82,000
Victoria beach air station	 90,000
Parry Sound and Whitney unit..	..	31,810
Ottawa air station	 49,000
Ottawa photographic section	 21,000
Aeroplane and engine repair depot..	38,000
Roberva.1 air station	 35,000
Dartmouth air station.. ..'	 9,000

The minister has let us have some light on some things that have been a mystery to us for some time as regards the merging of the three departments of Militia, Naval Service and the Air Force. He intimates to the committee now that, as regards the Air Force, the essential features are to 'be retained, which I assume to be the commercial or civil aviation features. As regards national defence, the Air Force is going to cease to exist entirely. The training at Camp Borden, the minister has informed the committee, is to be discontinued.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No, I did not.
Or, that he hoped to have it reinstated at a later date.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I did not say it was to be discontinued.

Then I misunderstood the minister. The Air Service is one that, I am afraid, the majority of people are inclined to underestimate. At the conference which took place at Washington some time ago between the great powers, one might have observed how readily the disarmament proposals which were made were being accepted by some of those countries, and at the same time the information
Supply-Air Board

came out-and it is undoubtedly the view of many of those countries-that the air force was going to be a much more prominent feature of warfare in the future than it had ever been in the past, and that possibly some of those nava'l armaments would not be so invulnerable as they had been in the past, and might possibly be a handicap. As far as I can understand from the minister's explanation, the Air Force, as a [DOT] defensive force, is practically going to cease to exist; the civil aviation is going to be continued if some arrangement can be made with the provinces to employ these people, who will be under the Department of National Defence, purely as a civil force, and the services of those men who attained1 such wonderful experience and training during the war will be dispensed with. The minister is apparently unable to give the committee the information which has been repeatedly asked for, because he does not know what arrangement he may be able to make with the different provinces in utilizing the force which would be under his control. I hope I have not misstated what the minister has said. The Departments of Naval Service, Militia and the Air Force are not being amalgamated into Department of National Defence; and so far as I can gather, the only body of, I will not say men, but of anything savouring of military training in this country, which body is going to be maintained and for which the estimate has been kept up, is that of the Boy Scout movement in Canada. Is it possible that the people of this country are going to depend on our boy scouts as a body of national defence in the future? The minister may smile, but this is a serious1 matter. While peace may prevail in this country at the present time, who knows how long peace may continue and how soon we may require the services of those men whom the minister is pacifically ignoring to-day and allowing to go back into civil life again? It is most important and essential that a number of these highly trained experts should be retained, so that this country might benefit from the valuable experiences which they have gained from the services iwhich they rendered to Canada, instead of allowing this to become purely a civil force.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I am glad to have my hon. friend speak in that way, because my great trouble during the past two weeks was in the opposite direction. The majority of people complained that I was making this all military and not leaving any civil force. As a matter of fact, praetfi-
[Mr. Sutherland.
cally all the aviators engaged in forest protection work are members of the Canadian Air Force, of the Defence force. This work which they do in doing civil aviation is for civil purposes, but it gives them possibly the best training they can get. They are really training for defence purposes in the work that they are carrying on. For instance, flying over the forests, photographing the ground Ibeneath, is just the work they would be doing on the battlefield. While civil aviation is to be carried on, the bulk of it will be carried on by members of the Civil Aviation Force who will get the best training in air work in that way.

I quite understand that the only men who are really competent to operate these flying machines are the men who have seen military service. But the minister has not denied the fact that it is becoming a civil force and is no longer a part of the national defence force at all. Why should men who are acting as fire rangers throughout the country be listed as part of the defence forces of the country? Yet that is what the minister is doing.

There is a very strong
opinion on the part of authorities throughout the country that there is a great deal of destruction going on in our forests, and I understand that part of this force is used for the purpose of protecting these forests. Possibly the minister at an earlier stage may have explained this matter thoroughly, but if he did I was not present. I should like him to give to the committee more in detail some of the work which is being done by the air force in the protection of forests. He might tell us how much work is being done in sections of the country where the natural resources belong to the Dominion, and in other parts where the provinces own their own resources, such as Ontario, British Columbia and Quebec. Thb is an important question which is engaging the attention of the people of the country to-day.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
We discussed that matter at great length. We have been doing work for the province of Ontario, for example, in the protection of forests, and also for Quebec and British Columbia. The activities of the force have been engaged in the Forestry branch, the Geodetic Survey branch, the Topographical Survey branch, the Dominion Water Power branch, the Parks branch, the Reclamation Service

Supply-Air Board
department, the International Boundary Commission and Town Planning branch, and the Geological Survey branch; and also in connection with the Department of Marine and Fisheries, the Department of Agriculture, the Department of Customs, the Canadian National Railways and the Department of Trade and Commerce. The force did some work for the Ontario government in forest protection, and, as well, for the provinces of British Columbia and Quebec.

What arrangement is
made, in regard to this work, between the Dominion government, and, say, the province of Ontario, which owns its own lands? Is there some arrangement by which the work is carried on partly by the Dominion government and partly by the province?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
We are running two
stations in Ontario, at Whitney and Parry Sound. The province pays the cost. Last year they paid $15,000. British Columbia last year paid $20,000. In Quebec there is a station built at Robprval. We took their construction of the station as their share of the work; but this year we propose to do the work on a return payment basis.

That is, they pay the
expenses.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.

The minister has given some stations where the cost is to be so much, totalling a very small sum, and he evidently desires to leave the impression that he is to have $625,000 saved by economies pending some bill which is to pass the Senate. Now, in the first place, the minister has been in departments long enough to know that all the amalgamation in the world will amount to a comparatively small matter compared to the cost of the services themselves. In fact, I doubt myself if it will amount to anything at all; I think it is mostly talk. For that matter, the minister could bring about the amalgamation under the law as it is to-day. The Air Board, under the statute passed a few years ago, could be moved into his department at any time; he does not need any bill for the purpose. But to say that he cannot tell what is to be applied to certain services, that is, how his officers estimate the application of this money, because he is awaiting the results of reorganization, is really to make a statement that cannot be accepted by any one who has had anything to do with departments. The minister
knows what services were rendered before by the departments under every head; and when he comes to this committee and says that he does not know what he intends to do as respects any service that last year cost so much money, but wants the committee to vote him the money and let him do what he likes, he is simply asking for a blank cheque. Details have been given in previous years, and reorganization-a matter of an accountant or a supervisor here or there-has nothing at all to do with the question of services rendered in these various fields, so that there is no reason why the information cannot be given. If I am wrong the minister will correct me, but it seems to me that he told his department to cut the vote to a million dollars. They saw they would have to have $75,000 for salaries, and in order to make up the reduction they have cut the second vote to $17,500, and the estimate for Canadian Air Force and Civil Aviation to $907,500. If they have not made up their minds as to how they intend to apply the money in the particular fields of service, as was done last year, then they are not prepared to come and ask for a vote. They should wait until they are ready to submit the figures to Parliament; but they need not wait for reorganization. They cannot cover such a multitude of sins with the pretext of waiting for the bill to pass the Senate. They should know, if they do not, what it is intended to apply in the various fields designated by the ex-Minister of Air Service. I really think they must have that information here. If they cannot give it with absolute accuracy, they could be accurate enough for all the purposes of the committee.

I represent a section of the country covering some
10,000	square miles, where forest fires are an annual occurrence. Tremendous losses are sustained in both Gaspe and Bonaventure as a result of these fires, and I am glad to know that an arrangement is being made with the provinces by which protection is to be given to the forests. I think that is the phase of the aviation service that will appeal to the people generally, because our forests are one of the most valuable assets of the country. Do I understand from the minister that this service is provided on application from the provinces, and that the arrangements rest with the provincial governments? Is there a patrol kept up regularly in the Gaspe peninsula?
Supply-Air Board

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Where the Dominion has no lands the province itself is responsible for the protection of forests. They call on the department to provide the service, for which they pay. We are now in correspondence with the Quebec government.

I do not intend to detain the committee, but I want to point out as a final protest that while we, as the people's representatives are deliberating on an item involving a million dollars, there is not one man in the committee, save the minister himself, who knows what is to be done with that money. Now, is that right? If we vote this money, every dollar of it can be spent for the militia of Canada, and there is nothing before the committee to limit the minister in any way in the expenditure of the money. We are asked to vote it blindly without any particulars except as regards two or three stations mentioned by the minister a few moments ago, which account for a small portion of the vote, and the general statement that work is to be done at High River and one or two other points. If we are to vote a million dollars without inquiry and without any definite information except the general statement that it is to be applied to the air service, I do not know why we cannot vote millions and millions of dollars without any details. I never saw a more blank vote asked for, and, if this committee passes it, I never saw a more blank vote given. I make my protest; I am not going to do anything more about it.

I am not sure that I fully understood some of the figures given by the hon. minister. I understood him to say that the expense of the High River patrol last year was $120,000, and that this year it was to be $82,000, and that he expected to be able to give the same patrol service as was given last year in that part of the country. It is almost impossible for me to conceive how he can do that unless there was much extravagance and waste in the expenditure last year. We are very insistent in our part of the country that the patrol system be maintained to the fullest extent possible, and even extended. I do not know how far the patrol extends, but I live pretty well south in the province, in the Lethbridge district, and I know we have had a number of very serious forest fires to the west of us in the Waterton Parks region. My recollection is that we have had such forest fires nearly every year. I do not think that the High

River patrol as at present constituted reaches that far, although I may be mistaken. If it does not, I deem it essential that, instead of being restricted, the High River patrol should be extended so as to cover the Dominion forests and parks clear to the international boundary line. That is essential not only to preserve the forests for their timber, but to ensure the success of our irrigation projects there, as the snow on the forest clad hills is the source of moisture upon which that part of the country depends in a large degree. I hope the minister will look into this matter again and see that at least there is no cut in the amount allocated to keep the patrol at High River in a state of the highest efficiency.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The difference is largely due to the fact that we spent approximately $30,000 last year in construction.

I would suggest
to the minister the advisability of letting this vote stand over until we have some definition of what " National Defence " really is. In the bill for the consolidation of the three old branches of the service I do not see any definition. If national defence in the future is to consist of an air force for forest ranging and the detection of smugglers, I think the House should know it, and that the Upper Chamber should also be so advised before the bill becomes law. To my mind national defence has an entirely different meaning from that of civil aviation for the purposes which have been outlined here. An air force undoubtedly is going to be a tremendously important factor in the defence of all countries in the future, much more so, I believe, than the average person realizes to-day, and it seems to me that you are dragging the service into the mire when you utilize it to detect smugglers and forest fires. The prevention of smuggling is essentially a work for the naval service-for the ships that are to be returned to the Motherland with the compliments of the Government of Canada. I quite agree with the late Minister of Militia (Mr. Guthrie) that we should have something more than this information so far given to this committee. If this money is to be expended on civil aviation, and the training at Camp Borden and elsewhere is to be abandoned, I think it is a very, very important matter and should be treated a little more seriously by the Minister of Militia and Defence.
