Item agreed to.
Naval service-to provide for the maintenance of the Royal Canadian Navy, $1,500,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in askin ; for the supply for the Naval Department for the ensuing year I think it is but fair
Supply-Naval Service

to the committee that I should explain that the money chargeable to the Naval Department is not expended entirely on the naval service proper. I will place on Hansard the names of the various branches of the department so that in discussing the estimates hon. members will understand that under certain headings we are asking for supply for services which have nothing to do with the Royal Canadian Navy.
We have what is known as the Royal Naval Service itself. Then we have the Fisheries Protection Service, which is composed of ten vessels,, two on the Atlantic, two on the Pacific, two on the Great Lakes, and four not in use at the present time. These patrol the coasts of Canada and are charged with the regulation of fisheries. The duties of that branch I will explain under the estimates relating particularly to it. Then we have the survey of tides and currents, a service that is highly technical, involving the preparations of tables, etc., for the use of navigation. Then we have the branch called the Hydrographic Survey, composed of four main parties and five ships. These operate on the lower St. Lawrence, gulf of St. Lawrence, southern coast of Nova Scotia, and coast of British Columbia. The duties of this service are the preparations of charts of the coasts of Canada, such charts being guides for mariners; the fixing of relative levels of the St. Lawrence system as a basis for the study of international relations on the river by means of chain of automatic gauges. Then we have what is protbably the most wonderfully developed branch, the Radiotelegraph Service. There are 43 radio stations owned by the Canadian government. On the eastern coast these are operated by the Marconi Company, who are subsidized by the Government; on the Pacific Coast they are operated by the Government. They have charge of the direction-finding radio stations on the Atlantic, at St. John Chi-bucto, Canso, and Cape Race, Newfoundland. This service administers the Radiotelegraph Act and has charge of all radio matters in Canada; issues licenses to all radio stations in Canada, commercial, experimental and amusement; issues licenses to ships equipped with radio; inspects all ships and stations to which licenses are granted; holds examinations for various grades of radio-telegraph operators; handles all accounts connected with radio matters.
The subject of the Canadian navy is one which has interested the people of Canada

for some years. In 1910 what is called the Naval Service Act was passed, under which Canada established for herself a naval service. In 1911, I think it was, arrangements were made under which the British Admiralty handed over to the Dominion certain services which the Admiralty had previously performed, particularly those relating to the docks at Esquimalt and Halifax. Now, there was great divergence of opinion as to what we should do under the Naval Service Act. That act, of course, provided for different things. Under it the then government purchased two ships, the Niobe and the Rainbow, for the purpose of training young men for naval service. The purchase was made in 1910, in consultation with the Admiralty. In 1911 the government changed, and in 1912 these ships were tied up. When the war broke out in 1914, the Niobe was refitted and placed in service, and served one year. Then it was taken out of commission and used as a depot shop, or something of that kind. In 1911, I think it was, an arrangement was made, followed by a treaty later, by which Canada agreed to do what Great Britain would otherwise have had to do in the matter of patrolling the waters of the Behring sea for the protection of the seal fisheries around the Pribyloff islands. The Rainbow was deputed for that service and she was steaming for these waters when the war broke out. She was brought back into naval service, and served during the war. In 1920 she was sold for $67,000 to some commercial firm, by whom she is still being used as a freighter. We had no ships to take the place of the Niobe and the Rainbow until the British government, after the war presented to Canada three ships, the Aurora, the Patricia, and the Patriot, and two submarines. The records of the British House of Commons disclose that a question was asked in the House as to whether Canada undertook to maintain these ships in commission when they were accepted, and the answer was, in substance, that there was no agreement except that implied by the acceptance of the ships. I think we are all agreed, notwithstanding any criticism that has been made, that Canada must maintain something of a naval service. We started such a service in 1910. It has passed through various vicissitudes, and I think the opinion now generally expressed as to what Canada must do in the matter of naval service is primarily to protect her own coasts and harbours, and her fisheries. We

Supply-Naval Service
showed during the war, although we had no navy, that Canada was ready to do her part just as well as any other portion of the overseas dominions, or as thoroughly as the Motherland herself or any of her allies, so there can be no question of the willingness and anxiety of the Canadian people to do their duty as a young nation in the making. What has been done in the past will be continued, I believe, in the future.
We are in this position in regard to the question of a navy. Every country in the world to-day is endeavouring to reduce its armament. At the great conference in Washington recently, where we were represented, the great nations of the world agreed not only to take a holiday in naval construction, but to scrap many of their fighting ships. All over the world to-day people are anxious to reduce as far as possible, within the limits of safety, and without any sacrifice of national dignity the expenditure on fighting machines and fighting material. Let me quote just a few sentences from the report made by our own representative at the Washington Conference, Sir Robert Borden, to show what the trend of public opinion is on this question. On page 17 of that report, in sessional paper No. 47, we find the proposals that were made for the reduction of naval armaments:
(1)	That all capital-shipbuilding .programmes, either actual or projected, should be abandoned;
(2)	That further reduction should be made through the scrapping of certain of the older ships ;
(3)	That in general regard should be had to the existing naval strangth of the Powers concerned;
(4)	That the capital ship tonnage should be used as the measurement of strength for navies and a proportionate allowance of auxiliary combatant craft prescribed.
I also want to read from page 80 of this report to show the trend of public opinion as represented by the great minds of the great powers of the world, and
5 p.m. to make it clear that the trend is towards a reduction in expenditure on armaments, without any sacrifice of national dignity and consistent with considerations of safety. Referring to the great powers the report says:
The treaty provides that all other capital ships of these Powers, either built or building are to be scrapped or disposed of as provided in the treaty.
It is provided that the present building programmes are to be abandoned and that there is to be no building of capital ships hereafter, except in replacement and as the treaty provides.
Let me pause for a moment to make a comparison with the proposal which was made on November 12 on behalf of the American Government in respect to capital ships.
That proposal set forth that 18 ships were to be retained by the United States, with a tonnage of 500,650 tons. In this treaty the same ships are to be retained.
In that proposal there were set forth 22 capital ships to be retained by the British Empire. Under this treaty the same number of ships is to be retained; in fact, the same ships, with the single substitution of the Thunderer for the Erin, with a tonnage of 580,450 tons, as against the calculation in the proposal of 604,450 tons for ships retained.
In the case of Japan, the proposal set forth 10 ships to be retained. By the treaty, the same number of ships is to be retained, the difference being that the Mutsu is to be retained and the Settsu is to be scrapped. The tonnage retained by Japan, as indicated in the proposal, was 299,700. The tonnage retained under the treaty is 301,320. The effect of the retention of the Mutsu, a ship just completed, on the part of Japan, was to make necessary certain changes for which the treaty provides.
The minister referred to the number of ships permitted to the British Empire. Would that include Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
It would include, I think,
all the overseas dominions.

Have we a
capital ship?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not think we have.
Then how can it include Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I said, the overseas dominions, and if Canada had a capital ship it would affect us.

We would benefit, of course, from having these 26 capital ships in the service of the Empire. Is Canada paying towards the upkeep of those ships? Is it because all nations in the world are moving to reduce their expenditure on armaments, as the minister has just read, that he is reducing this item to $1,000,000? Or did that apply to Canada, which practically, to all intents and purposes has no navy?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
It applies to Canada,
being one of the overseas dominions. As I pointed out, Canada has no capital ships. She does not contribute to the upkeep of the British Navy. No man in the world, I think, would agree more heartily than myself to the proposition that the British Navy is essential to the peace of the world. The British Navy not only saved Canada but saved our friends on the other side of the line, and it is a question of policy whether there should be a contribution, or

Supply-Naval Service

that each portion of the British Empire should do its own part. Canada at the present time has taken the ground that we, as a young country, growing up, having our own service,-the British government having handed over to us the naval service, which we undertook, and the management of our militia,-should proceed along that line. It may be in the years to come that Canada will have to develop, perhaps, a larger naval service than she has or has had, but one that will maintain the principle of Canada, within the Empire, being a nation that, so far as possible, looks after her domestic affairs. However in the times of stress and war, the British Navy is the safety of the world.

I should like to know from
the minister if under the Washington Agreement, it is possible for Canada to have a capital ship until the expiration of that agreement which will occur, I think, in 1940.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I would rather think
not.
Unless it were in reduction of Great Britain's capital ships.

We could
look after one of her ships.

We could not in Canada,
if we are bound by the terms of the Washington Agreement, build one capital ship until 1940, unless we did it through England.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I imagine, as part of the British Empire we could have one transferred.

No difficulty
about that.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
But I am not absolutely
sure that we will.

One reason that I asked
the question was that I noticed a statement in the paper by Lord Lee a little while ago that he was just a little disappointed that the whole burden of the 26 capital ships was going to fall on the taxpayers of Great Britain, who were already overtaxed. But, morally, I think we are responsible, because we are receiving protection, and if the members on the other side of the House, and we on this side of the House, are always saying that, as far [DOT] as we are concerned, we are a nation, and

that we want to stand on our own feet, I think we ought to help pay for the protection we receive.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
If we started discussing
that question, it would take us pretty far afield, because that is a pretty large policy, It has been said that certain things did take place at the conference of premiers. I do not know anything about that.

The resolution is on
the table of the House.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I am inclined to think
what is on the Table of the House is not everything.
It is everything:

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
It is everything that
is on the Table of the House.

It is everything, in
so far as Canada's engagements go.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I am not going to be led astray. Some day we may discuss that matter. I have a lot of documents in my desk relating to it. I was just reading part of the report of Sir Robert Borden of what took place at the conference at Washington, merely to point out to the House and to the country the trend of the public mind. I find the following in this report:
"The United States proposes, if the plan is accepted

one year's service for any period not exceeding six months, and for such further service he shall not be entitled to any increased rate of pay, unless, in the opinion of the Governor in Council, the circumstances of the case and the conduct of the person concerned merits it.
That is one kind of force. Then there is another which provides for a volunteer force, and I want to submit to the judgment of members of the House that, in the Dominion of Canada as we are now situated, a better service on our own behalf, a better service for the Empire at large, will be obtained and can be retained by using the voluntary effort of our young men better than by having a great permanent force. The act of 1910 provides for this. It reads:
The Governor in Council may organize and maintain a force to be called the Naval Volunteer Force.
The Naval Volunteer Force shall consist of officers and seamen raised by voluntary engagement from among seafaring men and others who may be deemed suitable for the service in which such volunteers are to be employed.
The Governor in Council may make regulations for the government of the Naval Volunteer Force
Every naval volunteer shall be engaged for the term of three years and, provided his conduct and qualifications are satisfactory, shall be eligible for re-engagement for further periods of three years up to the age of forty-five years; at the expiration of each term he shall be entitled to his discharge, save as hereinafter mentioned.
Naval volunteers shall receive such training and capitation or other remuneration as may be prescribed.
In an emergency the Governor in Council may order and direct that the Naval Volunteer Force, or such part thereof as may be deemed necessary, shall be called into active service, and the naval volunteers so called out shall be liable to serve under such regulations as may be prescribed.
If a naval volunteer's period of service expires while he is employed on active service, he shall be liable to serve for a further period of not more than six months, and for such further service he shall not be entitled to any increased remuneration, unless, in the opinion of the Governor in Council, the circumstances of the case and the conduct of the person concerned merits It.
In short, the proposal that I have to lay before the House, and for which estimates are asked, is that we discontinue in commission the ships that we now have; that we continue the protection and care of the wharves and docks at Halifax and Esquimalt; that we provide a reserve force composed of officers and men, officers who are now in the navy-the number of them altogether, I think, will be 233, if I remember correctly-that we create on the Pacific coast at Esquimalt an establishment with one small ship and two trawlers of about 450 tons; that we establish there a por-
[ Mr. Graham. ]
tion of our naval force for training in the protection of our shores, protection of our harbours, mine-sweeping, mine-laying; that at Halifax in the east we have the same services. I may say that we have the boats that we can use for this service economically. We have in contemplation the selling of one small boat that we have and the purchase of another which, if it can be secured at the same price as the other one is being sold at, will make an ideal ship for the Pacific coast, and Captain Hose tells me that it is just the ideal craft for patrolling the seal fisheries. We have not such a craft in the present group of ships. With these three at Halifax and these three at Esquimalt, we shall have, in those two services alone, ships, boats and crews that will give first-class training to young volunteers. In addition to these ships, it must be remembered that the second line of defence, if one might call it so, the great reserve in the Dominion of Canada, is our merchant marine. I do not mean altogether by that the merchant marine owned by the Government; but it includes all our wonderful merchant ships which during the late war performed such great services, a service second only to that of the great warships and, perhaps, in many cases not second.
Then we have the Fisheries Protection service, containing quite a number of smaller ships. We hope in time, if the scheme goes through and is successful, as I predict it will be, that we shall find an outlet for our young men whom we train in those ships in our own boats in the Fisheries Protection service. Further than that, as long as the Government continues to operate the merchant marine, I believe that will furnish an outlet for the young men so trained. This means that, under this estimate, in another year-it will take most of this year to get organized-some 1,500 men can be trained during the year on land and on sea for two or three weeks. These young men will not go to Halifax or Esquimalt at the same time; they will go at different times and receive their instruction, so that the officers will be kept busy most of the year. This will have one benefit, namely, that it will not take a single man out of industrial employment in this country. In a permanent force he is out of industrial employment and is a consumer and not a producer; but by this method the young men will get training on land and sea for two or three weeks per year over a period of three years just as the militia get train-

Supply-Naval Service
ing now for several weeks during each year. They will be given the rudiments the first year; the next year they will receive training in mine-laying and minesweeping; they will be taken out for a short cruise in the ocean and back again. This will have the effect of instilling into the minds of our young men that they can take a part in this work and train for naval service without leaving their own employment. They will be absent for only a few days.
It strikes me that another feature of this will be that, as part of the course, the regulation will require that these young men take a drill wherever they reside, of an hour a day for some few days in the year, at no cost to the country except, perhaps, that of an instructor from the department. This will not involve the expense, proportionately, that our military training has involved, for the simple reason that we have in all centres of the Dominion now armouries where this department, organized with the National Defence Department, will provide the quarters for the young men who wish to train, without the expense to the naval service. Newfoundland has a force of this kind; so has South Africa; and I believe that in preparing the young men in the way I have outlined, forming a volunteer force, we shall instil a better spirit into them because they will feel that they are doing the thing because they want to do it. I believe that in the years to come it will be shown that in taking this step we have begun at the right end of the problem. To my mind the problem of having anything like a naval service is not solved by getting one or two ships, and having a permanent force on them. The force at present consists principally of men from Great Britain; we have men of our own, of course. But this proposal will bring our own young men more intimately in touch with the naval service and so far as patriotism can be inculcated by that kind of service it will develop that spirit to a greater extent in our youth. I do not want to be prophetic, but should we require, in the years to come, to develop a navy, we shall have on hand in the Dominion young men trained to take positions in that navy. Under this scheme we are retaining four officers from the British Admiralty. The rest, kindly loaned to us, will return to the Royal Navy. The others will be young Canadians. I do not know that I can say anything further. This is the scheme we have in mind for the training of 1,500 men annually for this work and for which we now ask from the committee an appropriation of $1,500,000.

The minister's statement is important in this sense, that it touches a subject that is of paramount consequence to our whole country. It has been of great concern for years, and indeed will be so long as we are a country. I do not propose now to go into any detailed criticism of what are described as the proposals of the Government as related to naval service. They require careful examination, particularly at the hands of one who is not familiar with the question from any technical standpoint. I merely give now a statement of my view in a very broad and general way.
I was impressed, as the minister proceeded, with the thought that the Government's plan of defence is admirably adapted to guard ouh shores with absolute security throughout the days of peace and quiet. So long as there is no danger I am quite sure that this force which the minister proposes will be entirely adequate to meet any assailant. I am thoroughly in accord with the sentiment he uttered when he commenced his address, and I am only sorry that his concrete proposals have not the remotest relationship to that sentiment or to its inevitable consequences. Yes, in time of quiet and serenity the five trawlers will be all right and we shall be quite safe in training our navy in our armories. But in time of emergency and danger, which in my humMe judgment, as a layman, is really the time one requires to prepare against, then it is that defence is rather more desirable than in sunshine and calm. In such a time, though, we are to depend upon the British navy and the British taxpayer

I do not know of What value this Government's service is going to be. I wonder if the minister is armed with any statement, from one acquainted with the needs of empire defence, as to the value of this service? If he has such a statement I should 'be very glad if he would give it to the committee. It occurred to me, as he spoke, that it would be rather serious for us if Great Britain herself prepared for her and our defence in this manner, if she put a few trawlers on the Atlantic to watch the fish, and put a few boys into our armouries as a sort of diversion or pastime. If she took that course what would 'become of our defence in the hour of crisis and peril? Where would Britain be? Where would we be? No, she does not take that course; that in-
Supply-Naval Service

diligence is reserved for Canada. I am afraid the minister's statement will be received with profound disappointment, if not with poignant humiliation, on the part of this country.
The statement just given makes some comparison of what we are doing, with what South Africa has done. I fear his comparison will not hold good very far. South Africa is a very small country in population and a very young country compared with Canada. He also compared us with Newfoundland. I do not doubt the comparison is likely a very good one in the measure of what we are doing. I have no doubt, too, that possibly Trinidad and maybe Bermuda would be appropriate comparisons; but the minister omitted these two countries.
So far as our freedom of action is concerned, it stands to-day where it has always stood throughout our history. The position taken by this country last summer was embodied in a resolution agreed to unanimously by all the representatives of the nations of this Empire. It was a resolution which obviously expressed the right course, because the measure of imperial defence, essential could not he known until the measure of world armaments would !be dealt with by the Disarmament conference. The Disarmament conference is over, and now the time for determination of our policy has come. We are free to decide. This is the resolution that was passed:	i
That while recognizing the necessity of cooperation among the various portions of the Empire to provide such naval defence as may prove to be essential for security, and while holding that quality with the naval strength of any other power is the minimum standard for that purpose, this conference is of the opinion that the method and expense of such co-operation are matters for the final determination of the several parliaments concerned, and that any recommendations thereon should be deferred until after the coming conference on disarmament.
That was the resolution that was passed.
I should like to know from the right hon. gentleman if that resolution is to be taken as implying a contribution to the Empire by Canada for naval purposes.

Not at all; it is to be taken as implying just what it says. Let me read It again:
That while recognizing the necessity of cooperation among the various portions of the Empire to provide such naval defence as may prove to be essential for security-

The word used is "co-operation." There are many ways of )co-operation. The method is left absolutely open.
-and while holding that equality with the naval strength of any other power is the minimum standard for that purpose, this Conference is of the opinion that the method and expense of such co-operation are matters for the final determination of the several parliaments concerned, and that any recommendations thereon should be deferred until after the coming Conference on Disarmament.
Now, it would be well to proceed with the estimates for the purpose of obtaining any information that may be desired; but I do not think the discussion should be closed to-day. I think perhaps some time next week might be fixed when the discussion of the issue in its general aspect could be continued.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We might take the other branches in this department first, such as the Hydrographic.
Yes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I should like to ask my right hon. friend one question to clear up a matter of doubt which appears to be in the minds of a good many hon. gentlemen. I assume he has read the London despatch which appeared in the newspapers of the 10th instant of an address delivered by the Right Hon. Lord Lee, First Lord of the Admiralty, who was one of the British delegates to the recent Washington conference, before the Colonial Institute in London on the subject of the Washington conference. The despatch contains the following:
Lord Lee pointed out that the Imperial conference, after a full, prolonged, and intimate discussion of the naval needs of the Empire, had agreed that the maintenance of an Empire navy was the common concern of the whole Empire, and that the extent and form whereto the burden shSuld be shared should be left until after the Washington conference.
Is my right hon. friend aware of any understanding arrived at at the conference which he attended with respect to any obligation upon Canada in relation to an Empire navy?

I am certainly not
aware of anything beyond the resolution. That, I presume, is a press statement of what Lord Lee said. Lord Lee was doubtless interpreting for himself the resolution. There was no agreement or understanding of any kind whatever save that embodied in this resolution which has been on the table of this House since the opening of the session.

Supply-Naval Set-vice

Was that resolution not passed in the face of proposals similar to those suggested by Lord Lee in the newspaper report? In other words, were there not proposals made by the British representatives at that time for a contribution from the dominions?

I would have no difficulty whatever in answering the question if I could do so in honour. The conference published its report, and I am bound to abide by it. Those are the conclusions of the conference. I cannot go behind those conclusions until it is agreed that publicity can be given. The Government is in a position to obtain consent for such publicity, if it yet can be obtained. It has refused to try. Some things are confidential for a time, but do not need to be so for all time, and the seal of confidentiality can be lifted sooner or later. If the Government secure consent to lift that seal, the details of the proceedings at the conference can be known. Until then I abide by the report which is on the table, as I am in honour bound to do.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Are we right in assuming that the Canadian government is not obligated in any particular with respect to matters of imperial defence beyond what this Parliament has already approved?
The government is not obligated by me save to the extent disclosed in the document now on the table.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I ask the right hon. gentleman the question as one of the representatives of Canada at the Imperial Conference. Is he aware, directly or indirectly, of any obligation resting upon the government of this country as a consequence of the conference which he attended with respect to naval defence other than what has already been approved of by this Parliament?
I am aware of none, and there is none arising from that conference other than what appears in this document.
must face the situation in the light of the experience which these men have gained and which is embodied in the conclusions they have arrived at.

If I caught correctly what the hon. member said, I take no exception at all to the terms of the extract he read from the report. I would presume it was quite right that the Empire delegation at the Disarmament Conference was in no way entrusted with the power of decision in anything that related to co-operation among the dominions of the Empire in the matter of naval defence, and therefore I am in thorough accord with him. I think perhaps I have as good a right as any member of this House to express the fullest sympathy, indeed, enthusiasm, with all the purposes of the Disarmament Conference. That that conference did make it possible for the heavily burdened nations of the world to reduce their naval armaments is a matter for the sincere congratulation of all humanity. It is no doubt that it did take a very long and a very practical step to that end. As to what may be the residuum of necessary defence for this Empire, after all that is done, and as to what, the residuum fixed, may be our share therein, is another question. I venture to suggest that he would be a remarkable Canadian who would find our share taken care of in an honourable way by the estimates presented now, and by the proposals of the minister.

The right hon. gentleman may be enthusiastic with regard to the result of the conference at Washington, but he knows very well that the conclusions of the Imperial Conference were that this whole subject should be postponed until after the conference on disarmament at Washington had taken place, and that the question as to what participation there should be on a permanent basis should form the subject of another imperial conference. In the meanwhile, why should we not have a naval holiday, the same as every other country?
Until another imperial conference?
Yes.
But I did not understand the minister to say he was deferring the final pronouncement of his policy until there was another imperial conference.
Nor did 1 say so, either.
I thought we were getting the policy now. The naval holiday that the hon. member wants for Canada is only to last until the next imperial conference; is that what I understand him to say?

No; my right hon. friend is at his old trick of quibbling and hair-splitting. The point I am making is this: the effect of the resolution adopted by the conference which my right hon. friend attended last summer, and agreed to by all the delegates, was that the question of the participation of the overseas dominions in the naval defence of the Empire should be postponed for consideration until after the holding of the conference in Washington. That was expressly set forth in the resolution which my right hon. friend has read. Now, the conference at Washington has taken place; conclusions of a general character have been arrived at, and the absolute inference, having regard to the manner in which the question was dealt with by the Imperial Conference last year, is that its consideration is to be postponed until another imperial conference is held.

Well, if I was hairsplitting and quibbling I was only repeating the position which the hon. member himself had taken and which he has now repeated. That is what I understood him to say before. The resolution that was passed did not postpone the determination of the part to be taken in imperial defence by any dominion until the next imperial conference. It says :
That, while recognizing the necessity of cooperation among the various portions of the Empire to provide such naval defence as may prove to be essential for security, and while holding that equality with the naval strength of any other power is a minimum standard for that purpose, this conference is of opinion that the method and expense of such co-operation are matters for the final determination of the several parliaments concerned, and that any recommendations thereon should be deferred until after the coming conference on disarmament.
Who are going to make the recommendations?

The recommendations referred to there would doubtless be recommendations by another imperial conference if it chose to make any, but it does not say by any means that nothing should be done pending another imperial conference. If this Government is saying that it is waiting for recommendations from an-

Supply-Naval Service
other imperial conference, then perhaps my hon. friend's words would have some application. Does the hon. member say that they are waiting, before making a declaration of policy, for the findings or recommendations of the next imperial conference? The hon. member, when I suggested that, resented it with some heat.
That is what the Imperial Conference wanted the overseas dominions t*o do-to wait until another conference was held.

Not at all; this resolution means just what it says. But, I say, if the Government were to state-which it does not-that it is waiting before coming to its conclusion for another conference, possibly the comments of the hon. member would have some relevance. But the Government does not say so; the hon. member himself affirms that the Government does not say so and that he does not say so. The Government has come down with its policy, as it had a right to do; it was not in any way bound to wait by the terms of the resolution of last summer. It has come down with its policy, and that policy is now before us for our consideration.
May I ask the right hon. gentleman what these recommendations which he has read refer to?
To the method of cooperation with the other dominions and with Great Britain as to naval defence.

Do they not also imply
the expense on the part of each nation?
What imply the expense?

The recommendations.
The right hon. gentleman has, in his resolution, mentioned the expenditure and the method.

The recommendations
can cover anything that another conference decides to recommend upon.

I would like to ask the right hon. gentleman whether in his opinion this Government is under any obligation to advise a policy prior to any recommendations which may come from a subsequent imperial conference? It seems to me a rather strange thing that the Government should attempt to lay down a policy prior to the holding of another conference. Does the right hon. gentleman think the Government would be wise or justified in taking such a step at the present time?

I do not think the
question arises, because the Government has taken the step. The minister has made no reference whatever to waiting for another conference; he has announced his policy, such as it is.

I am very glad to hear
the leader of the Opposition say that the resolution to which he has referred does not involve this country in any obligation, and I accept his statement in that connection so far as contribution is concerned. But I am frank to say that while I have been able to read only the summary of the speeches of the premiers of New Zealand and Australia, they seem to bear a somewhat different construction. I think, Mr. Chairman, that we should have an opportunity to discuss this matter very fully in order that we may determine exactly our position and exactly what our obligation may be in the future.

Mr. Rankin-Mr. Gordon in the Chair.

I should like to say a few words in connection with this bill. I do not want the committee to think I am criticising their work in any way, but I think this bill passed the committee in somewhat of a hurry, as the committee was in session only about twenty minutes. This company, which goes under the name of the Canadian Transit Company, wants to change its offices from Windsor, Canada, to the American side, and I think we should look into this bill a little more carefully before we pass it. We must stand up for the good name of Canada, and if any company comes over here in order to get prestige from the name of Canada, I think Canada ought to be good enough for it and to keep, its headquarters in. Not only do the directors of the company want their headquarters transferred to the other side; but they want to sell bonds in Canada and when they do so, they want to have the right to mortgage the property. I know, on a number of occasions when this sort of thing was carried out in British Columbia, bonds were sold up to pretty nearly the limit of what the company intended to do. They sold the bonds to people who did not expect that there would be anything crooked about the matter. They sold the bonds to men working for $30 a month. I know men working for that amount who invested over $2,000 in such a company. They then mortgaged the property and allowed the mortgage to lapse, so that the people lost everything they had. I do not think this bill should be passed as it is. I do not think it has had the consideration

I suggest that the Government consider the question of cost. The cost of maintaining the telegraphic land line to the Yukon is, I always did think, prodigious. I remember bringing the matter up more than once and asking the officials to go thoroughly into it with the view of determining the possibility of establishing wireless stations. The cost of upkeep would surely be infinitely less than the cost of the upkeep of a land line.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The department has discussed that with the Public Works Department on more than one occasion. I think they have a scheme practically worked out, but it has never been consummated. I agree with my right hon. friend that it would be cheaper to maintain a radio service than to meet the annual cost of repairs and upkeep of the telegraph line.

I may say for the
benefit of the minister that the strongest
pressure will have to be brought to bear upon the officials of the Public Works Department. They have had it under consideration-and I kept prodding their consideration-for a long while, and that under a live minister. The minister will have to keep very busy indeed if he is going to get any results there.

In connection
with the suggestion that the radio be substituted for the present land line to the Yukon, known as the Yukon telegraph line, I think myself that the Government might very well seriously consider such a proposal, but not with the view of altogether scrapping or abandoning the Yukon line, because in the Yukon territory its operation and maintenance is economical. That part of it is not subject to the heavy storms or weight of snow with which the part of the line in northern British Columbia has to contend. An examination of the accounts and expenses of upkeep will show that fully eighty-five per cent of the cost occurs south of the Yukon boundary in northern British Columbia. I think it would be altogether in the interests of economy if that Yukon telegraph line could be disconnected from its southern connection at, say, the new mining camp of Atlin in British Columbia, or at White Horse in the Yukon Territory. The line from there south to the National Transcontinental is practically of no use except as a connecting link, and on that portion of the line the greatest part of the expense occurs. There is practically no revenue from it. The stations are isolated; supplies for upkeep of service and maintenance of operators have to be carried over hundreds of miles on pack-horses, with consequent high cost for both maintenance and repairs. Double shifts have to be maintained at these stations, they are so isolated; it is not safe to have only one man, as is done in the Yukon. Now, from the National Transcontinental west to Prince Rupert that government telegraph line is duplicated by the National Railway telegraph line. There is no need whatever for two lines from that point of contact west to Prince Rupert. If the Government would establish one radio station either at the mining town of Atlin, British Columbia, or at the mining town of White Horse in southern Yukon, they could cut out all that expensive stretch of land line. The sooner this is done, the sooner they will commence to save money and bring about greater efficiency. For weeks at a
Supply-Naval Service

time nearly every winter that line is down; the people of the north country are cut off from communication, and are obliged to send their messages by radio or by cable around to Alaska and Seattle. I would very much regret the taking of any step which would remove the telegraph line within the Yukon territory, connecting, as it does, points along the trail and along the river, affording means of communication for steamboats in trouble along the river, and providing communication between the mining camps. I may say that I am negotiating with the Public Works Department in an endeavour to have them extend that line within the Yukon Territory for a distance of some 75 miles from the main Yukon telegraph line to Mayo. More business goes over that section than over any other part of the line, and leaving out of consideration the expense of maintaining the line through British Columbia, that section is a paying unit, and the proposed Mayo branch would undoubtedly pay and handle a great volume of business. The Mayo branch would undoubtedly pay and handle a great volume of business. I therefore wish to support the remarks that have been made in favour of establishing a radial station in northern British Columbia or southern Yukon, which would make unnecessary that very expensive telegraph line to the south connecting with Prince Rupert.

Supply-Naval Service
to the retention of Wrangel island or the continuance of Canada's claim thereto; and the same words apply to the other islands covered by the expedition.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The policy of the Government, as I understand it, is as just expressed by the Minister of Finance-what we have we hold.
Well, have we Wrangel island?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, as I understand it, and we propose to retain it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We had it in December, and we have not let it go.

I think there is probably, as the leader of the Opposition has said, a great deal more to this matter than appears on the surface. I understand that the United States have published a map in which they show all the lands north of Melville island, I think, as being a country which does not belong to anybody, and which is consequently open for discovery by any nation whose expedition may happen to locate there. I think it is a matter of the utmost importance that we should not lose sight of the fact that the extreme northern part of this country should be preserved to Canada. It may not seem of much importance now, but I have no doubt that in the years to come it will be a matter of very great regret if this or any other government fails to take proper measures to ensure that that country belongs to and is secured and maintained by Canada.

I can only say in addition to what has been said by the hon. member for West Oalgary, that this question is being discussed in the United States papers now. Within the last month it has been discussed in the New York Times and the Washington Post, and there is no doubt that certain interested parties in the United States intend to make a claim to Wrangel island as United States territory by right of prior discovery. In my view, from the little inquiry
9 p.m. I have made, I am satisfied that that claim is unfounded. There is no right of prPr discovery beyond the right of Canada or Great Britain in that respect. However, this matter is going to come to the front in the very near future, and I think it is high time that this Government should take a stand on the matter, and make its stand known to the world!
It will be a matter for international discussion very soon unless we are going to forego our claims and let the United States take over the island. Whether the island is of very much practical importance I do not know, but parties in the United States seem to think it is. In fact, one paper says that from one point of view, the mineral wealth of Wrangel island is far greater than that of Alaska. That may be problematical, but it is the basis of the claim which is made by certain interests in the United States.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The Government has had interviews with Mr. Stefans-son. I do not know that it is in the public interest to disclose the full nature of those interviews, but I might say that at the present time the Canadian flag is flying on Wrangel island, and there are Canadians on the island, members of a previous expedition of Stefansson's. Mr. Stefansson is about to take a ship up to Wrangel island with some of his men, and has recently had it fitted out with supplies. The Government certainly maintains the position that Wrangel island is part of the property of this country.

That is clear and definite. Of course, the Prime Minister knows that the men that were there were there long before he had been in his present position, and therefore some considerable length of time. I may say as well that there may be claim to this island on behalf of Russia, a claim based very largely on the geographical location of the island. The island of Ellesmere on the west coast of Greenland is also one to which the Government should give some attention. An expedition was about to be launched by a Dane, with, I think, the approval of the Danish government, designed to make some occupational claim in Ellesmere island, and it was anticipated, probably, to base on that occupational claim certain rights of Denmark in the island. I call that matter to the attention of the Government, so that whatever position Canada is in with respect to Ellesmere island will be held, because, in my judgment, Ellesmere island is of greater consequence than Wrangel island.

This is a matter of intense interest to every member of this House. Some subjects are discussed, and those who take part are able to speak in a loud tone. This is a matter of great interest, and yet this whole discussion is

I suppose the committee understands that these war claims that are now being paid under the heading of "adjustment of war claims" were formally carried in the estimates under an item called "Demobilization vote." The name has been changed, but the purpose of the item is just the same. This claim arises out of the late war. There are a number of claims, I fancy, not ready for settlement.
I had occasion last year to enter into a controversy and discussion with the Ministry of Shipping in England in regard to their claims against the Dominion of Canada. What I want to know is whether the item now under discussion is one of the items which were taken into account which we adjusted last summer. I may say that after three or four weeks of pretty hard work, in which I had the very able assistance of an accountant from the Militia Department, we succeeded in reducing the claim of the Ministry of Shipping by an amount of $750,000, and we agreed upon a stated amount for the various items that were chargeable against capital, but the account had to do very largely with the question of passage money, and damages to ships while in the Canadian service. It was purely a shipping account, I cannot remember just what the figure of the total account was, but there was one very serious outstanding claim which I refused to settle, and I hope it has not been settled yet. It was in connection with a boat which was submarined, and which was in the hospital service of the Dominion of Canada at the time at which it was submarined. The case had been referred in England to a board of arbitration upon which Canada was not directly represented. The finding of the arbitration board was that Canada must pay the replacement value of the ship, and I think that value was something like $5,000,000. The ship was certainly chartered by Canada, or by the British government and used by Canada at the time of the disaster. The cost of the ship was about half that amount, and, in the first instance, when the Admiralty dealt with losses of that kind, they allowed the cost of the ship, but after a few months' experience, with an allowance of that kind, the same board of arbitration changed the basis of allowance and allowed the cost of reproduction, and, as the cost of construction of vessels had risen enormously in the interval, Canada was let in by the arbitrators finding for an award of something like a million or twelve hundred thousand pounds, but, as Canada was not

Supply-Naval Service
represented directly on the board-we were nominally represented by some department of the Admiralty-I objected to the payment of that amount, and I assume the amount is still outstanding. My object in mentioning it now is to bring it to the attention of the minister, because I think that is one of the claims that should be very seriously reconsidered before it is allowed. The other claims I dealt with were all shipping claims, and the account with which we were dealing was adjusted after a reduction of $750,000. Does this item involve the matters which were settled by the representatives of the Admiralty and myself and Mr. Garrison of the Militia Department last summer?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is not in this expenditure. I think you will find it in the Militia Department.

There was some uncertainty. The Admirality made a claim against Canada for a million dollars which they said the naval service of Canada owed them, and they requested authority to deduct it from the settlement of accounts, I had no authority to agree to that and I thought perhaps it was this $1,900,000 which we had before us.
Something was said by the minister as to a claim on account of the difference in exchange. It was some $200,000, was it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service

speechtext:
How does
this arise?

I understood the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) to say that the British government were seriously asking the Canadian government to become responsible for the loss of this hospital ship that was sunk by a German submarine. It seems to me that a claim of that kind would be absolutely absurd, and I join with him in saying to the minister, that I hope the minister will never acknowledge any such claim on the part of Great Britain against Canada.

We have not acknowledged it, but there is something in the contention that we are liable for something in the matter. When we took over ships as hospital ships, we took them into the service of the Dominion of Canada, and we became responsible for them and for all the wear, tear and damage. The
rates got so high that it became impossible to insure these ships. The British government abandoned insuring ships and we did likewise; in fact, I do not know that we ever attempted to insure them. We have, however, paid losses on ships under our control which were sunk by submarines. The point that struck me was that we should not be liable for anything but the actual value of the craft sunk, and that was only 50 per cent of the amount found by the board of arbitration.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
If my recollection in reading over some of the documents in the department serves me aright, some of the settlements were made through the High Commissioner's office; but the details, to which my hon. friend refers, I imagine, I have in the Militia Department somewhere.
As regards the question asked by the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton), the British Admiralty sent us drafts on New York instead of on Montreal. We really received more money than we should have received, because wa got the benefit of the exchange on the American currency. They are now making a claim for the amount of exchange.

I hope that will not be given into at all, because at the same time that we received drafts on New York, if I remember correctly, they also insisted on our making payments in New York at the New York rate. I also remember very distinctly that the British Admiralty took full advantage of the New York rates; and if we have taken advantage of them, we have only been acting in accordance with the same rule. I think the item should be struck out.

My hon friend knows
that the decision in this matter lies with the Department of Finance. Although this item is inserted, we do not propose to pay the claim unless we are instructed to do so by the Finance Department after investigation. By inserting the item in the estimate, we do not admit the claim at all; but should the Finance Department, after investigation, decide that this claim is good, we have provided the money to settle it.

It seems to me that it would be better to settle the matter in this way, namely to advise the Finance Department that we do not think there is any claim; and if a new claim has

Supply-Naval Service

to be looked after as a result of different advice, it may be dealt with by a Governor General's warrant. I do not think it should be admitted even to the extent of inserting the item in the estimates. We have a claim for a very much larger amount which England as steadily declined to admit. Unless I am very much astray in my recollection, I think the fact is that we have already settled cross accounts with the Admiralty on the basis of New York exchange, and I think, therefore, no action should be taken in this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is a large question between this Government and the British government in connection with the matter of exchange, and we must be prepared to give and take; whatever we lay down on one side we expect to claim on the other. My impression is that, if this claim be approved, it would require an appropriation of Parliament to pay it. Therefore, my hon. friend may be wise in inserting the item, but I quite concur in the view that he had better not be in a hurry to make payment until the whole matter is adjusted.

I certainly agree that he should not be in a hurry to make payment. I am quite sure that the whole matter will be property and fairly adjusted. When it once gets to the British government and out of the routine of the offices, I do not think there will be much difficulty in adjusting the matter. I have no doubt, when the Prime [DOT] Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) takes a very well earned holiday this summer and goes over to England, he will be able to adjust the whole of this matter without any difficulty.

I think the minister said, in explaining the details of this item, that part of it was for war medals. The department issued a war service badge which was very unsatisfactory, and1 many complaints have come to the Minister of the Naval Service and his officials. I have received, in the last two or three years, probably two or three hundred letters from young men who received this war service badge which was issued to men Who served in the Canadian navy or to Canadians who served overseas in the British navy. The badge was very much larger than the one issued to the soldiers, and these young men claim that it should be similar to the one issued to soldiers, instead of the large white badge which was issued by the Naval Department. I have, upstairs in my room, about a dozen of these badges which weye

sent to me by these boys. They would not keep them, and they asked me to bring the matter to the attention of the Minister of Naval Service and to ask him to have issued a new badge which would be satisfactory to them. They want one the same size as the one issued to the soldiers, which badge was quite satisfactory. This will cost a very small sum of money, and these young men, who risked their lives on the sea, should receive some consideration from the Government. I trust the Minister of Naval Service will look after this matter and issue the badges to the naval men.

I understood the minister to say that one of the items contained in this very large appropriation is for reconditioning or repairs to certain vessels, known as drifters. We had a very large number of most curiously constructed, queer looking vessels floating around the coast of the maritime provinces. I do not know where they were built, and anybody who knows about conditions there knows they were of no value during the war. I cannot understand why we should be now voting money for vessels of that kind. Some of them belong to the Canadian Government, but I do not know whether there were brought across the Atlantic any that belonged to the Imperial government.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
As a matter of fact,
these were trawlers or drifters that were built in Canada on the order of the Imperial government and lent to Canada. The contract with the Imperial government was that we should repair them and place them in the same condition as they were before. None of these items, of course, will be paid without the fullest scrutiny.
With regard to the medals, I must admit that the medals issued by the Naval Department have called forth a good deal of protest. Many that were issued by the British Admiralty were large. The Naval Department, I understand, has issued some that were smaller; but so far as I could learn, neither the larger nor the smaller were quite satisfactory. We will go into the matter and see if any alteration can be made in the design of the badges.

Mr. Chairman,

Are these furnishings replaced from year to year? I imaging that most of the members who are familiar with the debate on the necessity for economy must be somewhat startled when they observe the elaborate furnishings which have been brought into this building during the last two or three weeks. Throughout this country in past years there have been built by both governments expensive and elaborate public buildings in different towns and cities. I admit that in the capital city, such buildings should be in keeping with the dignity of government, but in some towns and cities it seems to me they are too large and too elaborate and might well be subdivided in order to afford more space for use as public offices. I have in mind some cities, including my own, where there are immense buildings for the Customs D*
Supply-Public Works

partment while other branches of the public service are spread over the city in rented quarters. It has been my impression that not only in my own city but in others, there would be plenty of room for other departments if these large buildings were further divided up. I am not blaming the present Government in the least, for most of these buildings were erected years ago; but in some of the customs offices I have seen there seemed to be enough room to provide for the needs of cities five or six times the size of those in which the buildings were situated. Possibly the minister would do well to carry on the work that was taken up by Mr. McCurdy, who, I happen to know, was looking into the possibilities of co-ordinating or bringing together some of the different offices of government. Of course, I would not like the minister, in return for my suggestion, to carry out the idea in my city alone.
Use that for a starting point.

No, not even as a starting point. But I would be quite willing to see my city taken with the rest of the cities in anything which is done in this connection. I think the minister would be well advised to carry on the work that Mr. McCurdy started to do, but which he did not have an opportunity to complete.

I shall be very glad to give that matter consideration. It is advisable wherever possible to bring these various services under one roof. My hon. friend suggests that he would like any action taken with respect to his city to synchronize with similar action in others. We will bear that in mind.

I find in a return which was brought down at my request on the 20th of April last, that coal was imported from the United States for use in federal buildings as follows: in 1918-19, 28,973.91 tons, at a cost delivered of $318,850, or an average cost per ton of $11; in 191920, ,32,646.81 tons, at a cost delivered of $327,941.65; in 1920-21, 52,279.58 tons, at a cost delivered of $821,748.55, or an average cost per ton of $15.71. In other words, while the Public Works Department imported in round figures, 29,000 tons of American coal in 1918-1919, at a cost of $319,000, or an average cost per ton of $11, this tonnage increased for the year ending March 31, 1921, to over 52,000 tons or nearly double the quantity, at a cost of nearly $822,000, or nearly treble the cost in 1918-1919.
The leader of the Opposition has spoken to-night of some Canadian coal being used in the public buildings in Ottawa. Very little could have been used, because under his government and its predecessor the amount of American coal imported for the use of public buildings jumped inside of three years from 28,000 odd tons to 52,000 odd tons per year. Is it the policy of the present Minister of Public Works to discontinue using American coal in federal buildings where Canadian coal can be procured at a decent price?
Yes.
When that was done in 1920-1921, Canadian Companies were not in a position to supply the coal. Was not Canadian coal bought last year for the public buildings?
Yes.
Of course it was, and what was the proportion?

Replying to the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan), the date he stopped at was the date up to which there was an ample market for Canadian coal elsewhere. In Ottawa the policy was established-I cannot give the exact date, but certainly all the time I was Prime Minister, and I think before-of buying Canadian coal rather than American coal because the prices were so comparable we could do it. So I was right in what I said. The time came when the market for coal overseas was exhausted, and what did the late government do? We pressed on the railway companies to buy Canadian coal to keep the men employed. They, of course, resisted because the price was higher, but we stood behind the company and paid the excess price out of the treasury of Canada in order to keep the men employed to the utmost extent we could during that hard period. That was the course the late government pursued in all these things, and I think it was right. What is more, I would do it again.
I believe we ought to use Cana-
10 p.m. dian coal. There is a limit, of course. You cannot go very far above the market price at which you can get coal elsewhere, but we can afford to do something in order to extend further the market for coal produced in our own country.

The hon. gentleman's argument would be all right if his facts were right, but perhaps he does not know quite as much about the coal trade as we who come from the province of Nova Scotia. I can tell him that when he purchased 52,000 tons of coal in 1920-1921, as compared with
28,000	tons in 1918-1919, the bottom had then dropped out of the coal market and the miners of Nova Scotia were walking the streets.

That was not last
year.

The bottom dropped out of the coal market in 1919, after the armistice in 1918, and in 1920-1921 coal was an absolute drug on the market and our miners in Nova Scotia were unable to secure employment. It may be hard to explain why in that year the amount of coal imported from the United States was almost twice as much as the amount imported three years before.

I do not know that we will gain much unless we get the real facts. They ought to be here. I asked the minister how much Canadian coal was bought last year for use in Ottawa, and how much American coal.
The figures I am quoting are from a return brought down to the House, so there cannot be any doubt as to the correctness of the figures.
The hon. member gave the figures for 1920-1921. What were the figures for last year?	.

It was in 1920-1921 that we had a lack of coal orders in Nova Scotia. I am as anxious as the ex-Minister of Finance to hear the reply of the Minister of Public Works. The ex-Minister of Finance has rather intimated that this is not a matter of importance.
I rise to a point of order, Mr. Chairman. I never said any such thing. I think it is a matter of importance, and it is important that we get the facts.

The amount involved may not be stupendous, but the principle involved is a very important one. In my humble opinion the time has come in this country when we must establish a Canadian national coal policy, and it must be the rule of this Government, not only for its public buildings, but for the railways, to purchase coal mined in Canadian mines. Look at the item before us. The government of Canada, for the year ending 31 March, 1921, bought over $800,000 worth of American coal for use in its own public buildings. Do hon. members think the United States of America would buy Canadian coal to use in their public buildings? At Washington they would almost sooner burn wood than Canadian coal.
We need in this country more Canadian-ism and more devotion to Canadian industry. We preach the doctrine, which is all right in itself, to buy Canadian goods made in Canada, but we often forget to buy coal produced in Canada. It is one of our natural products. Upon it depends a large amount of the revenue of the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, and yet we will find that, even down in some cities in the maritime provinces, large quantities of American coal are being brought in, and burned and very often burned by those who are preaching the loudest "buy goods made in Canada".

This is in my humble judgment, a most important matter, although only involving perhaps a few hundred thousand dollars. At the same time, it is important in principle that it should be established in this country that we should patronize Canadian home industries, particularly those that are producing from our natural resources. We had a statement made here not long ago, in answer to a question by the hon. member for Pictou, (Mr. Macdonald) in reference to the amount of American coal burned on Canadian railways, and I think the answer was "about a million tons per year". Do hon. members realize the fact that down in the province of Nova Scotia-and I presume this remark applies to the western country as well-about two thirds of our collieries are idle, that men are walking the streets looking for work, and at the same time the government of Canada is buying a million tons of coal per year for railway purposes? According to this statement, for the year ending 31 March, 1921, we burned a million dollars worth of coal in public buildings. This is not Canadianism, and not a policy which will build up Canada, particularly that part of Canada which depends so largely upon the production of this very important product of our country.

I entirely
agree with my hon. friend from Cumberland (Mr. Logan) in the principle he has enunciated. The late government went so far as to practically pay premiums for Canadian coal, and they were criticized for it in this House. I am amazed at one statement my hon. friend makes. He tells us that down in the maritime provinces American coal is being burned. If it is true that any one of our public institutions is burning American coal where Canadian coal could easily be got, the least my hon. friend can do is to give the facts to this House. Let us'know what the institutions are and where they are, because frankly I am amazed to hear the statement.

I think the hon. member may have misunderstood me. I did not say the government of Canada was buying coal for use in maritime cities from American sources. I said American coal was being burned in those cities by people who were preaching very loudly the "made in Canada" doctrine. I was amazed not long ago to pick up a Halifax paper and to see that they congratulated, I think, the

Supply-Public Works
school commissioners for having purchased a very large amount of coal, but when I came to consider the kind of coal it was, I found it was American coal being burned in the city of Halifax, in that province which depends so much on the production of coal. What we need in this country, in reference to coal and in reference to many other products of the country, is more Canadianism, and we should patronize Canadian industries as far as possible. There may be cases where it would be too expensive to bring in Nova Scotia coal, say to central Canada. That is another question, but, as far as the portion of Canada east of lake Superior is concerned, there should be no coal purchased by the government of Canada for use on the railways or the public buildings, except coal produced in a Canadian mine by Canadian miners.
Mr. ME1GHEN: I have only one word to say, and it is not in criticism of the hon. gentleman. fuel oil, so that our mines in Canada would have a better chance to give steady employment to our miners.

States in 1920-21 to the extent of $800,000, as mentioned by him. What kind of coal was that? Was it bituminous or anthracite, and could it have been purchased in Canada?

The return brought down in answer to my motion does not specify how much bituminous or how much anthracite was imported into this country. Now, I submit, that there is no necessity for importing any American coal for public buildings and government railways in Canada east of lake Superior, because bituminous coal, which can be used in the heating of all furnaces, can be purchased in Nova Scotia and in New Brunswick. The coal that was purchased for Ottawa by the late government was bought in New Brunswick and not in Nova Scotia. I make that statement by the way. Coal can be purchased in Nova Scotia at the present time, delivered on the government railways, at about $5.50 a ton. The Government owns the railways; they own railways running throughout the province of Ontario; and if they would carry coal at cost from Nova Scotia they could deliver it at the eastern end of lake Superior in competition against American prices. But they cannot do so if they charge the regular cost of transportation on coal. A few years ago the Government of Canada carried coal from Nova Scotia to the city of Montreal at $1.60 a ton. They increased the rate from $1.60 to $3.80. We contend that that is an excessive freight rate, but they would never suggest that it was the exact cost of transportation and my contention, even in opposition to what has been intimated by the minister, is that there is no need for this Government to buy any American coal for use in Ontario if they will only buy it in Nova Scotia or New Brunswick and transport it at actual transportation cost. They can buy a million tons of coal to-day in Nova Scotia delivered on the government railways at $5.50 a ton, and good coal at that.

I am not criticizing for
one moment the purchase of coal in the maritime provinces; quite the opposite. But to reach an intelligent conclusion regarding the criticism offered by the hon. member (Mr. Logan) with reference to the $800,000 expended on coal in the United States, it is necessary to know whether that coal was anthracite or bituminous coal. If it was bituminous, then the criticism might be well founded; if, on the contrary, it was anthracite, there was no ground for the criticism. And the same argument would apply to the discussion on some of the other items.

I contend that there is no necessity for buying anthracite for public buildings, and that is why I want the minister to tell me how much anthracite was bought last year for use in heating public buildings in Ottawa.
I have the information. There were purchased 163 tons of anthracite.

I am informed that the late government let a contract to a company in my constituency for supplying all the coal used in the public buildings here, and I understand that the contract price is lower still than that named by the member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan). I believe that coal is being loaded in New Brunswick, under contract made by the late government for the heating of public buildings in Ottawa, at as low as $5.25. I am glad the minister is laying down the policy which he has stated. It would be a great benefit to the district I represent and, incidentally, to the district he himself comes from. I do not see the necessity for buying anthracite coal, because in the lower provinces the use of anthracite in large public buildings is being entirely discontinued.

Any government coal
bought from the operators in Nova Scotia for the use of the Government should be transported at cost. It is not giving any advantage to the operators.

I received telegrams about a fortnight ago from people in my constituency complaining that American soft coal was being sold in the town of Windsor at about $4 less per ton than Canadian coal produced in Nova Scotia. Now, I claim that the railways of the country ought to be run on a business basis, and
Supply-Public Works

if you are to give special consideration to coal produced in any part of Canada the people generally will be taxed in consequence. Coal is not entitled to any greater consideration than any other commodity produced in the country. My reply to my own constituents was that the object was to get coal at the cheapest possible price and not at the expense of the public at large, and that they had to put up with it, and I was very glad that they were able to get coal for $8 or $9, as against $15 which has been charged during the past few years. My advice to the Government is to buy coal where it can be purchased at the cheapest possible rate. If that is done the Minister of Railways will be able to administer the railways of the country as a business proposition. If the railways give special concessions to coal it will mean so much more of a deficit; and I repeat that it will be the part of wisdom for the Government to procure their coal where it can be got at the cheapest price.
I should like my hon. friend to go down to Pictou and Springhill and some other places down there, and preach that doctrine at election time.
I am not afraid to preach it.
I am sure you have not the courage to do it.

I have the courage to practise whatever doctrine I preach, and if you come to my constituency and advocate that any special concession should be made in favour of any coal company in Canada at the expense of the consumer I will run against you. I will even go into the old Tory county of York and run an election there against the hon. gentleman.

No one is advocating any special concessions in favour of coal sold to the public. But the member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) contends that the Government in hauling its own coal for public buildings should do so without a profit, and he is quite justified in that contention.

The Government should be run on a business basis and the railways should not be hewers of wood and drawers of water for anybody. They are public utilities which are supposed to serve the interests of the people, and nothing should be done whereby the taxpayers can be mulcted in unjustifiable costs. I repeat that coal should be got at the cheapest price no matter where it comes from.

I am quite sure the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) is amazed when he finds the tremendous amount of anthracite tonnage -163 tons-which the late government imported into Ottawa. There was a reason for it: the late government was very sincere in trying to bring about a condition that would enable as much of our own coal as possible and our money kept in the country. Among other things we looked into the changing of our furnace equipment so that we could use bituminous coal, and in that way help our own coal mining industry and our own unemployed. City by-laws, of course, make *a good deal of trouble in some instances, but I dare say we will be able ultimately to use still more of our own coal. What business will be taken up on Monday?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The first
item of business will be concurrence in the reports of Committee of Supply, and putting the Supply Bill through the different stages. Then, as mentioned earlier in the day, we will take up the motions of private members that appear on the Order Paper, beginning with No. 23, relating to oleomargarine, and, when that has been disposed of, we will take up the other motions in the order in which they appear.

Has my hon. friend considered whether or not we shall have any choice as to how those motions are to be taken up? Is that not left entirely in the hands of private members? Are they not to be taken in their turn? I would have thought so.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I spoke of it this afternoon, and asked if there was any objection, and I understood the House was unanimous. I presume anything the House may agree to will he permissible.

I do not know. Perhaps the House did come to an agreement. I was not here at the time. If we had to come to any agreement, I would have thought that we would have agreed, at

Dominion Elections
least, to give preference to the motion for redistribution. I would have no difficulty in agreeing that my hon. friend should give preference to that motion on Monday.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I mentioned, in answer to the hon. gentleman who asked the question, that that motion would be taken up at a later time, but the Government would like to fix its own time for it. I wish also to mention to my hon. friend- and I mention it now so that hon. members will know

that on Tuesday we will go on with the estimates on naval service and continue with the militia estimates.
Motion agreed to and the House adjourned at 11.15 p.m.
Monday, May 15, 1922.
